{{Short description|Concept in geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[geometry]], a '''polar space''' of rank ''n'' ({{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 3}}), or ''projective index'' {{nowrap|''n'' − 1}}, consists of a set ''P'', conventionally called the set of points, together with certain subsets of ''P'', called ''subspaces'', that satisfy these axioms:

* Every subspace is [[isomorphic]] to a [[projective space]] {{nowrap|'''P'''<sup>''d''</sup>(''K'')}} with {{nowrap|−1 ≤ ''d'' ≤ (''n'' − 1)}} and ''K'' a [[division ring]].  (That is, it is a [[Desarguesian]] [[projective geometry]].)  For each subspace the corresponding ''d'' is called its dimension.
* The intersection of two subspaces is always a subspace.
* For each subspace ''A'' of dimension {{nowrap|''n'' − 1}} and each point ''p'' not in ''A'', there is a unique subspace ''B'' of dimension {{nowrap|''n'' − 1}} containing ''p'' and such that {{nowrap|''A'' ∩ ''B''}} is {{nowrap|(''n'' − 2)}}-dimensional.  The points in {{nowrap|''A'' ∩ ''B''}} are exactly the points of ''A'' that are in a common subspace of dimension 1 with ''p''.
* There are at least two disjoint subspaces of dimension {{nowrap|''n'' − 1}}.

It is possible to define and study a slightly bigger class of objects using only the relationship between points and lines: a '''polar space''' is a [[partial linear space]]  (''P'',''L''), so that for each point ''p'' ∈ ''P'' and
each line ''l'' ∈ ''L'', the set of points of ''l'' collinear to ''p'' is either a singleton or the whole ''l''.

Finite polar spaces (where ''P'' is a [[finite set]]) are also studied as [[combinatorics|combinatorial objects]].

==Generalized quadrangles==
[[File:GQ(2,2).svg|thumb|Generalized quadrangle with three points per line; a polar space of rank 2]]
A polar space of rank two is a [[generalized quadrangle]]; in this case, in the latter definition, the set of points of a line <math>l</math> collinear with a point ''p'' is the whole of <math>l</math> only if ''p'' ∈ <math>l</math>. One recovers the former definition from the latter under the assumptions that lines have more than 2 points, points lie on more than 2 lines, and there exist a line <math>l</math> and a point ''p'' not on <math>l</math> so that ''p'' is collinear to all points of&nbsp;<math>l</math>.

== Finite classical polar spaces ==
Let <math>PG(n,q)</math> be the projective space of dimension <math>n</math> over the finite field <math>\mathbb{F} _q</math> and let <math>f</math> be a reflexive [[sesquilinear form]] or a [[quadratic form]] on the underlying [[vector space]]. The elements of the finite classical polar space associated with this form are the elements of the [[Isotropic quadratic form|totally isotropic subspaces]] (when <math>f</math> is a sesquilinear form) or the totally singular subspaces (when <math>f</math> is a quadratic form) of <math>PG(n,q)</math> with respect to <math>f</math>. The [[Witt's theorem|Witt index]] of the form is equal to the largest vector space dimension of the subspace contained in the polar space, and it is called the '''rank''' of the polar space. These finite classical polar spaces can be summarised by the following table, where <math>n</math> is the dimension of the underlying projective space and <math>r</math> is the rank of the polar space. The number of points in a <math>PG(k,q)</math> is denoted by <math>\theta_k(q)</math> and it is equal to <math>q^k + q^{k-1} + \cdots + 1</math>. When <math>r</math> is equal to <math>2</math>, we get a generalized quadrangle.

!<math>n + 1</math>

!Notation
!Number of points
!Collineation group

==Classification==
[[Jacques Tits]] proved that a finite polar space of rank at least three is always isomorphic with one of the three types of classical polar space given above. This leaves open only the problem of classifying the finite generalized quadrangles.
